book.about: In Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, a single pint of stem cells flown in from Germany dripped into John Vallely's bloodstream while his blood count stood at zero. The Pyramid Principle is the true story of a former UCLA basketball player, NBA first-round pick and Houston Rocket who faced opponents tougher than any he met on the court. It begins on Balboa Island in Newport Beach, where a boy too small and too slow shot a thousand shots a night in the alley behind his house, and follows him through high school and Orange Coast College to his dream of playing for Coach John Wooden. Then life moves past the hardwood: his nine-year-old daughter's cancer and the family's loss of her at twelve, a courtroom battle with a bank, and Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma, and then a rematch with it. Through every struggle he turned to the guidance he had relied on since college, the words and teachings of John Wooden, the coach he considers the greatest teacher of his time. It is a story of love, loss, faith and perseverance, and of a family that kept saying, We are still a family.

sections.h2: For sports fans who want the story behind the jersey
paras: If you love basketball memoir, this is the view from inside Coach Wooden's program. John was named captain of a UCLA team the press wrote off as "The Team Without," after key players left for the NBA. He writes about the Bruins' routines, Wooden's lessons, teammates such as Kareem, and the road from Orange Coast College to Westwood. It ends with his induction into the UCLA Hall of Fame.

sections.h2: For families walking through childhood cancer
paras: Erin was nine when she was diagnosed and twelve when she died. John writes about the treatments, the hospital, the wig that floated off in a hotel pool, and her determination to go to a Father and Daughter Valentine's Dance. It is told as one father's testimony, not a manual. If you are in that hospital hallway now, you will find company in these pages, and you should also know it does not hide how much it hurts.

sections.h2: For survivors, and anyone fighting a battle they did not choose
paras: John fought Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma twice, and the book carries you through the diagnosis, the transplant and the rematch. Along the way he fought a long lawsuit against a bank with only a small legal team beside him. Whatever your battle is, the question he keeps returning to is the same: what does it mean to have done your best?

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who need hope in a hard season
paras: A basketball memoir that does not stay on the court. The Pyramid Principle is the true story of John Vallely, a former UCLA basketball player, NBA first-round pick and Houston Rocket. It moves from a boy shooting in an alley to the hardest opponents of his life.
Five things set it apart:
list: It starts in a stem cell transplant room. The book opens at Houston's MD Anderson Cancer Center, where a pint of stem cells flown in from Germany drips into his bloodstream while his blood count stands at zero, then goes back to the beginning to show how he got there.

It is built on a teacher's wisdom. John calls Coach John Wooden the greatest teacher of his time, and the book returns to Wooden's Pyramid of Success, with a quotation from Wooden opening several chapters.

It tells the loss honestly. His daughter Erin was diagnosed with cancer at nine and the family lost her at twelve. John writes that the earthly pain of loss is as great as ever, and he writes of the comfort of heaven in the same pages.
It refuses a shallow idea of winning. Success, he says in his Hall of Fame speech, is not wealth, power or position as the world defines it, but the peace of mind of knowing you did your best.
It is a family story. His son Eric told him, "Dad, we are still a family," and the book is dedicated to Eric.

paras: This incredible journey all started with a dream, a ball, and the sweet sound of a one-dribble pull-up and a basketball swishing through a hoop. It is a sound that is so pure, so soothing, a satisfying reward for executing the perfect shot: no rim, no backboard, nothing but net. The ultimate dream would be executing the ideal shot for the legendary Coach John Wooden and the Blue and Gold of UCLA.

In 1935, my father bought a bayfront property for $7,000 in the Southern California town of Newport Beach. He built bedrooms for my sister and me then hung a backboard up on the garage. Initially, my family complained about the constant sound of the ball bouncing off the basket. After years of dedication, my shot was so smooth that the noise could only be described as calming. Even my dribbling sounded rhythmic. Whether it was on the alleyway asphalt or the hardwood floor, that sound would change my life and one day lead to hope. During those years, I would spend hours upon hours in the alley shooting baskets, intoxicated by the sound and relentless in my efforts to hear it again and again.

stories.h2: The boy who was too slow
paras: At Corona del Mar High School John was 5 feet 3 inches and 104 pounds, undersized even for a guard. Years of shooting in the alley made him a great shooter, and he grew six inches in his sophomore year. By his senior year he was 6 feet 2 inches and leading his team in scoring. His own mom, he says, told him he was too slow. A letter of interest from UCLA, signed by Coach Wooden, then arrived, with a catch: he needed a 3.0 GPA, and his was 2.9. Karen, who would become his wife, told him, "You can do this, John."

stories.h2: Nine hundred people for one little girl
paras: After Erin died, nine hundred people came to her memorial service at Saint Andrews Presbyterian Church in Newport Beach: nurses, doctors, teachers, friends and children from the community. John knew he had to speak and did not know if he could hold it together. He writes that as the choir sang "Amazing Grace," it felt like heaven came down to the church. Years later, the family joined the "Dribble for Victory Over Cancer" event, where Erin was the honorary captain and every athlete pinned the name of someone they loved to their shirt.

stories.h2: A fight in a downtown tower
paras: John's legal case against a bank was, in his words, "going uphill and sideways." He found a one-man law office in Costa Mesa and a lawyer who greeted him with, "I was a big fan of your days at UCLA." The chapter is named for the question Coach Wooden asked: "Are you right?"

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: John writes that while he lay in that transplant room, in despair, he needed a way to hold on to hope in the face of uncertainty. "As I wrestled to find God's strength for my weakness in this battle, my only recourse was to turn to the same source of guidance and wisdom I have used for every critical struggle in my own life: the words and teachings of John Wooden, my UCLA basketball coach and a man I consider the greatest teacher of his time."

So the book is a record of what he learned and where it led. In the final chapter he writes, "I know in my head and from my experience that heaven is real," and "I still struggle and question. I'm still learning and growing." It is honest about faith in the way the best testimonies are: no tidy answers, only a man still choosing joy each day.

sections.h2: For anyone who knew Beetle, and anyone who did not
paras: If you knew him, you will hear his voice: the movie quotes, the Rubik's cube in his hand, the "Saweet!" he said when something went his way. If you never met him, you will feel as if you did. Dana writes him as warm, humble and quick, with a smile that said "I'll do anything for you" without a word. Friends, family and coworkers add their own stories at the end, from a school bus left in a ditch to a hardware store where every total was "a Thoooousand dollars."

sections.h2: For readers who love funny true stories about friendship and practical jokes
paras: Act I is all pranks. A teenage Stephen and Dana move a youth leader's car to the wrong side of a church driveway while a conference is under way, then wait to hear what happens. Later chapters go treasure hunting with a metal detector, fish for metal with magnets and set out on a bigfoot hunt. The humor is gentle, the friendship is the point, and the faith is never bolted on.

sections.h2: For readers who want to finish well, and anyone losing a friend
paras: Dana's closing hope for you is to "finish well in the race in which you find yourself." The last third follows Beetle through a hospital stay in Maine, a solved Rubik's cube, hard news from a physician, and a homecoming to his own house and his dog, Max. It does not hide the loss. It also does not let sorrow have the last word. This is one friend's story, not a grief manual, and you will find company in it.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want laughter and faith in the same story
paras: The Beetle Experience is a funny memoir that is not shy about the hard parts. Dana calls it "not a traditional memoir" and "not a conventional stage play either." It is something in between, and it welcomes you into the front row.
Five things set it apart:
list: It is a memoir-play hybrid. Prose memories sit beside dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues, vignettes and short Reader's Notes that give the time and place, so the book can be read quietly or staged with friends.
It is told by the best friend. Dana was there for the pranks, the summers at camp and the hospital room, and he narrates as himself, turning to the audience to give you the backstory.
It keeps its promise to tell the truth. "The stories you will see are true," Dana writes. "The names haven't been changed to protect the innocent as there were likely none that were innocent."
It lets you laugh and grieve in the same breath. In Beetle's last days, a room full of visitors is telling funny stories when he says, "I'm dyin' over here… and you guys are tellin' jokes!"

It ends with an invitation and a chorus of voices. After the epilogue come simple next steps for anyone who wants to start following Jesus, then "Last Words" from family, camp friends, coworkers and neighbors who knew him.

paras: In the summer of 1988, Dana, Stephen and a friend named Scott arrive as volunteers at Living Waters Bible Camp. A loud, laughing staff member named Ty Hutchins hands out nicknames to everyone standing in the dinner line. Dana is "Crash." Scott is "Pee Wee," to his fury. Stephen becomes "Beetle," because his last name is Bailey. Then the camp's assistant director, Roger Black, insists that he gave the name first. Dana settles it by asking the audience to vote and concludes, "I guess Beetle just… named himself." The same scene gives us the day Beetle tells a camper he is 45, and keeps saying it for years.

stories.h2: Captain Kidd's treasure, or what is left of it
paras: Every summer Dana and Beetle plan the fun they will have when he is back in Maine. One year Beetle has heard a rumor that Captain Kidd buried treasure near Wiscasset, so they take an old metal detector to the water behind his parents' house. They find spent .22 casings, a shotgun shell and a bottle cap. Dana admits that historians doubt Kidd ever reached the Maine coast, but says that without the rumor "he and I might have had some great memories stolen from us." The next summer they research a real abandoned gold prospect near Danforth.

In the hospital in June 2023, Beetle reaches for the Rubik's cube on his bedside table. His hands tremble, but he works it click by click until the colors line up, and Dana sees a verse come alive: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." (2 Timothy 4:7) A few scenes later, the room explodes into laughter at Beetle's line about dying, and the laughter dissolves into tears. Dana writes that in one line Beetle gave them permission to hold both, "the comedy and the tragedy — side by side."

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: Dana says the book began as a collection of memories, "funny, raw, sacred, and real," about a man God used to shape his life. Every time he tried to write it as a plain memoir, it felt "too small." Beetle, he explains, "isn't a man who speaks in paragraphs. He speaks in stories. Scenes. Punchlines. Pranks." So he started staging the memories, and the book became a hybrid.

"Some stories are too full of laughter to be told quietly. Some lives are too bright to be dimmed by paragraphs alone." It is an honest tribute, built on Proverbs 17:22 and on the belief that Beetle's joy pointed past himself to Christ. The epilogue says it plainly: "He ran his race, and he finished with joy."

faq.q: What is The Beetle Experience about?
faq.a: It is the story of Stephen Michael Bailey, known as Beetle, told by his best friend, Dana Morrison, as a memoir-play hybrid in six acts: a laughter-generating, treasure-hunting, churchgoing bundle of joy and the friends and family around him.

faq.q: Is it a memoir or a stage play?
faq.a: Both and neither. It is a memoir-play hybrid, with prose memories, dramatic scenes, stage directions, tableaux, monologues and vignettes that can be read, remembered, performed or passed along.

faq.q: Is it a funny memoir?
faq.a: Yes. It tells of pranks, tall tales, treasure hunting and a man who made everyone laugh, and it is rooted in Proverbs 17:22, "A cheerful heart is good medicine."

faq.q: Is it a spiritual memoir?
faq.a: It is a Christian memoir. Faith runs through the camp years and the final days, and the closing pages invite readers who want to follow Jesus, with simple next steps, such as reading the Gospel of John and finding a church family.

faq.q: Does it include practical jokes and pranks?
faq.a: Act I is built on them, from moving a car at a church conference to "Operation Indian House," and Dana says the stories are true.

faq.q: Is it set in northern Maine, and what is the Bible camp?
faq.a: Much of it takes place in and around Danforth, Maine, and at Living Waters Bible Camp, where the friends volunteered the summer of 1988 and where Stephen got his nickname.

faq.q: Will it help if I am losing a friend?
faq.a: It follows a friendship through Beetle's final days and homecoming, and it holds laughter and loss together. It is one friend's testimony rather than a guide to grief.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Anyone who knew Beetle and anyone who did not, readers who enjoy funny true stories with faith and friendship at the center, and readers who want to be inspired to finish well in the race they are running.

paras: In her late twenties, Cindy works in a hospital billing office in Walla Walla, Washington, and visits patients in her free time dressed as a clown. One day she is asked to come see a frightened toddler named Benji, who is in a full body cast and will let no one near him. When he sees the clown, his little body relaxes and he smiles for the first time. She leaves him a Polaroid of the two of them. Later that day he does not recognize her without the makeup, until she holds up the picture and says, "Benji, look. I am the clown." For six weeks she visits on her breaks, and on the day he goes home he tells her, "I love you too."

Driving to go Christmas shopping with a friend, Cindy hears a song on the radio and cannot shake it. She tracks down the recording, adds sign language she learned partly because her mother was hard of hearing, and asks her pastor if she can stage it with children before the service. He agrees, nervously. She appears as Sparkle in the middle of a congregation that is mostly elderly. When the song ends and she kneels by the cradle, the room bursts into applause and calls of "Amen."

Asked to perform for an entire school in Adams, Oregon, a town of 389 people, Cindy dreads the high school assembly most. The older students turn out to be the best audience. She invites two strong volunteers to push a fifteen-inch needle through a balloon. Theirs pop; hers does not, because she was prepared. The trick carries a message about preparing for life, and she follows it with "The Torn Heart," a paper heart she tears apart and then shows made whole again, to talk about what love can mend.

paras: John spends nearly four decades believing his pain means he is defective. He calls the sleepless nights, the startle responses and the headaches stress, anxiety and bad nerves. Then a trauma-informed therapist explains that Complex PTSD comes from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, "what happens when the people meant to protect you are the ones who cause you pain." For the first time, the chaos makes sense. He stops asking what is wrong with him and begins asking what happened to him.

At thirty-six, running a fast-growing business and traveling constantly, John wakes with his heart pounding and his chest tight. He ends up in the emergency room convinced he is dying. The physician comes back smiling. "Good news," he says. "Your heart is perfect. It's probably just stress." John writes that the physician was right, but not in the way he thought: "It was unresolved trauma that had been simmering for decades." The chapter becomes an invitation to listen to the body instead of silencing it.

Years later, volunteering at his hometown high school as a successful businessman, John sits in a small-group discussion when a mistreated teenage boy looks at him and says, "God doesn't love everyone. He plays favorites." John sees himself in that boy: the same hollow ache and quiet despair. He realizes that his success has not healed him, only distracted him. He writes, "That was the day I stopped running from my past."

paras: John says he wrote the book because he does not want you to wander as long as he did. "I don't want you to blame yourself for things that were never your fault. I don't want you to feel alone in symptoms that millions of people experience but rarely talk about."

He also gives a plain reason for writing about something so painful: "Because pain loses power when it's spoken out loud. Because healing grows when it's shared." faq.q: What is Invisible Wounds about?
faq.a: It is John Boyle's account of living nearly four decades with Complex PTSD he could not name, and a four-part guide to understanding it and walking the road to healing. The subtitle is Understanding and Healing from Complex PTSD.

faq.q: What does the book mean by complex PTSD?
faq.a: In the author's words it is "a disorder of reactions," and it "is not about what is wrong with you; it is about what happened to you." He explains that it develops from chronic, inescapable stress, usually in childhood, rather than from one event.

faq.q: What does the book say about hypervigilance and fight, flight, freeze?
faq.a: Part Two shows how trauma lives in the body and rewires a child's brain for fight, flight, freeze or fawn. Hypervigilance, startle responses and panic are among the experiences the author describes in his own life.

faq.q: Is it about childhood trauma and men's mental health?
faq.a: Yes to both. It follows the effects of a chaotic childhood into adulthood, and it speaks directly to male survivors, who are taught to push through alone.

faq.q: Does it explain emotional flashbacks and toxic shame?
faq.a: It does, in Chapter 3. John describes "gray days" that turned out to be emotional flashbacks, and he separates guilt from shame: "Guilt says, 'I did something wrong.' Shame says, 'I am something wrong.'"

faq.q: Are there exercises for calming the nervous system?
faq.a: Yes. Survivor Insight exercises help you name pain and replace self-blame with accuracy, and a 5-4-3-2-1 grounding reset helps when the body goes into panic or freeze mode. The resources section adds a five-step plan for day one.

faq.q: Is Scripture part of the healing?
faq.a: Scripture and prayer run through the book. Psalm 34:18 carried John through many dark nights, and the resources section lists verses for healing and hope. Faith appears as rescue, not doctrine.

faq.q: Is it a clinical book, and who is it for?
faq.a: No. The author explains what is happening without diagnosing and without overwhelming; it is a personal and faith-friendly account, not medical advice or a treatment guide. It is for anyone who has asked why they react so strongly, for survivors of childhood trauma, and for readers who want a faith-friendly account of recovery.

book.about: The morning starts like any other for four brothers. Their mother is cooking pancakes, Asher is full of questions about the orange sky, Elijah is tying his shoes, Samuel is checking the weather, and David is quietly humming. A warm retelling for young readers about sharing and trust.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers who want a Christian novel with a real hero and a real villain

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The book is a story, and it lets the story speak. It is built on two verses that Pastor Whittington's congregation heard on a hot August morning and that George remembers late in the book: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord," and "For the love of money is the root of all evil."

Those verses are the book's questions. What does one compromise cost? What do envy and greed do to a friendship? And, in the final chapters, what does mercy look like when it is offered to someone who has not earned it? The novel holds out the hope that God's mercy reaches further than our mistakes.

stories.h2: A sermon, and a life verse
paras: On August 30, 2009, just weeks after the diagnosis, Dan watched a sermon at the family cabin. The message was on Isaiah 41:10, and he writes that it "changed my life." The verse became his Life Verse: "So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with my righteous right hand." It came two weeks before surgery, "exactly when I would need it most," and he still prays it before major tests.

stories.h2: One in the morning, day eleven
paras: Ten days after surgery, Dan was not improving. On Saturday, September 26, 2009, he could not sleep for pain. He writes that he turned his head and saw Jesus by his left shoulder, with a woman beside Him he later understood to be Mother Mary. He was in St. Mary's Hospital. According to Dan, Jesus said, "Today you will have a very rough day, but you will get better." That afternoon he vomited blood and lost consciousness, and Kay ran into the corridor calling for help. He writes that the visit "dramatically changed the level of my faith and trust in Him."

stories.h2: The message at the supper table
paras: Years of chemotherapy had passed when Dan, at a July 2021 appointment, asked his doctor, "How would I know if I still have cancer?" A liver biopsy followed on July 29. Two days later his family was together at a restaurant when his phone chirped with the pathology report. The lesion was benign. "I have been healed; I am cancer free!" he told the table. He also records that his children were skeptical at first, and that they shared a wonderful meal and believed, at the very least, that their dad would be around much longer.

stories.h2: The king who bowed to a priest
paras: When Alexander the Great reached Jerusalem, the high priest was frantic with fear that he would destroy the city. That night he saw in a dream the gates open, the people in white and the priests in their robes, and he asked everyone to recreate the scene. Alexander stopped his army, rode up alone, dismounted and bowed. Asked by an officer why he, before whom people showed adoration, would honor a priest, he replied that he honored, not the priest, but the God the priest worshiped. Jerusalem was not attacked.

Origen was born in Egypt around A.D. 185 and tutored by his father, and he learned to quote long passages from the Bible when he was only a boy. He asked so many questions that his father reproved him for being too inquisitive, yet "secretly thanked God for such a child." When Origen was seventeen, his father was arrested and killed because of his faith. The youth tried to join his father in death, but his mother kept him home by hiding his clothes. He went on to head a Christian school in Alexandria and to compile the Hexapla, a massive book of Bible translations set in parallel columns.

Augustine preferred the theater to church, and his mother, Monica, prayed and wept almost continuously for him. She asked a priest to talk with him, and he answered, "Leave me and go in peace. It cannot be that the son of those tears should be lost." In Milan, Augustine began attending Ambrose's church only to study his eloquence, then found he could not ignore the meaning. The book prints Augustine's own account of weeping beneath a fig tree: "How long shall I go on saying 'tomorrow, tomorrow'? Why not now?" Then a child's voice nearby chanted, "Take it and read, take it and read."

book.about: Why do we celebrate leaders so often, yet rarely acknowledge the followers who make their success possible? The idea took root at a leadership conference at West Virginia University in 2007 and grew through a 36-year business career, years of mentoring from accomplished leaders and hundreds of interviews on his weekly podcast, Positively West Virginia. Followership, he argues, is not passive obedience or a fallback role but an active, intentional skill that demands humility, courage, loyalty, critical thinking and initiative. The book draws on biblical wisdom, from Joshua serving under Moses for forty years to Ruth following Naomi and Peter following Jesus, and closes with Jesus Christ as the greatest follower. Additional resources include the Humble Influence Roadmap to becoming an effective follower.

paras: In the opening chapter, a mentor named Mr. Doug hands the young author a Bible open to Joshua. Joshua led battles, carried out Moses' instructions and watched, up close, what leadership cost, including the day twelve spies went out and only two came back with faith. When Moses died, God chose Joshua. The author draws one conclusion: the mantle was not handed over by chance, it was earned through years of faithful service. A friend named Angela shows the same pattern in a modern office. She spent fifteen years under a demanding chief executive, studied how he decided, supported his vision, and was the natural choice to succeed him.

Lisa has an MBA and big plans, and a trainee program that has her shadowing department heads and compiling reports. She grumbles, "I didn't endure years of case studies and late-night group projects just to follow others around." Then a senior executive, Mr. Reed, tells her where he started and says, "Leadership isn't just about making decisions—it's about making informed decisions." Lisa begins asking questions in marketing and operations, and three years later she is asked to manage a struggling department, which she turns around within a year. Looking back, she decides her time as a follower "wasn't a detour—it was a masterclass in leadership."

stories.h2: Who cares who gets the credit?
paras: Chapter 11 opens in a marketing agency. A team leader named Lisa, in the middle of a client pitch, pauses to say that the concept would not exist without a colleague's creativity on the visuals. The room responds with admiration, and her team sees what kind of leader she is. The chapter pairs that scene with John the Baptist, who drew a large following and still said of Jesus, "He must increase, but I must decrease." The author's point is that great followers care more about the success of the mission than about their own recognition.

why.title: Why this book exists
paras: The author traces the book to a coffee shop in New York City, where a young professional named Michael told him, "Everyone talks about leadership, but what about people like me?" That conversation was the spark. He writes that "Over the years, I've met countless individuals who feel overshadowed by the leadership narrative."

He also saw a gap: "Surprisingly, resources for followers are scarce." His answer is a book that is not about stepping out of the shadows but about understanding the role you already play. In his words, "This book is a celebration of followership." It is meant for "the quiet contributors, the team players, and the behind-the-scenes problem-solvers who know that their work matters just as much—if not more—than the person at the top."

faq.q: What is Humble Influence about?
faq.a: It is a faith-grounded guide to followership for people who do vital work without holding the top title. Jim Matuga argues that following is an active, intentional skill, not blind obedience.

faq.q: Is it a book about biblical humility?
faq.a: Humility is central. The author names humility to serve without seeking the spotlight as the first trait of great followership, and the book closes with Jesus Christ as the greatest follower, whose submission to the Father's will became the path to ultimate leadership.

faq.q: Is it about servant leadership?
faq.a: It is about following rather than leading. Chapter 14 does look at Jesus as a servant who "did not come to be served," but the subject of the book is the strength of true followership.

faq.q: What does it say about Joshua and Moses?
faq.a: Joshua served under Moses for forty years before leading the Israelites into the Promised Land. The author uses that story to show that following prepares a person to lead, because Joshua learned discipline, empathy and humility along the way.

faq.q: Does it cover Ruth and Naomi?
faq.a: Yes. In chapter 5 Ruth chooses to follow Naomi back to Bethlehem. The author quotes her words, "Where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay," and points to her gleaning in the fields as proof that she followed with initiative, not passively.

faq.q: Is it about leading without authority or leading from the middle?
faq.a: In spirit, yes. The book is for people who want to lead "from the middle," to serve quietly and to influence with humility without a formal leadership role.

faq.q: Is it a Christian leadership book?
faq.a: It is a Christian book about the other half of leadership. It draws on Scripture, including Joshua, Ruth, John the Baptist, Peter and Jesus, alongside history and real-world examples.

faq.q: Who is it for?
faq.a: Quiet contributors, team players and behind-the-scenes problem-solvers, and anyone who wants to lead well by first learning to follow faithfully. It has fourteen chapters, an epilogue and a Humble Influence Roadmap.

sections.h2: For readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: If you are tired of explaining yourself, this book does not ask you to. It asks you to sit down at the well. The author tells her own failures without excuses and then shows, chapter by chapter, where she found grace. You can read one chapter at a time, write your answers on the questions at the end, and pray the prayer when you are ready.

sections.h2: For anyone who has asked what a loss did to their worth
paras: The author writes about a belief that took hold after her first heartbreak: that she was "unworthy of anything better than what I had lost." If that sentence sounds like something you have thought, you will find company here, and you will find the story of a woman in John 4 who was treated the same way and was met by Jesus anyway.

sections.h2: For personal study and small groups

Groups that want to talk about shame, forgiveness and judgment will find plenty to open up.

what_makes.title: What makes this book for readers healing from divorce and broken relationships
paras: A devotional in nine chapters, built from one woman's story and from Scripture. It opens with an allegory of a place called Virtue, moves through shame and failure, sits for a long chapter with the woman at the well, and ends with steps toward moving forward.
Five things set it apart:
list: It does not excuse and it does not condemn. The foreword says the book does not praise or justify one of the most divisive subjects in the church, and that "it points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices in life."
It is told by someone who has been there. The author writes that after "Thirty years, three marriages, and five kids," she had failed herself, her father and God, and she says so plainly.

It stays close to Scripture. Chapters draw on Genesis, John 4, the Psalms, Isaiah, Romans, Paul's letters and more, quoted from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles, with the references listed at the start of each chapter.
It is built for journaling and groups. Every chapter ends with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, then a prayer.

stories.h2: A well walled in with stones
paras: The allegory begins in a sanctuary of meadows and a clear stream, with a well as pure as a young girl's heart. A young man draws close and then slowly pulls away, and a storm follows. Years later, after much loss, the author describes herself as guarding her heart so fiercely that "I encapsulated the well with thick, impenetrable walls, built up with stones of fear and distrust." At the gate she staked a sign with a new name, "Vulnerable, population: one." The chapter ends with questions that ask readers where they see themselves in the picture.

stories.h2: Jesus sat by the well, and He waited for her
paras: In Chapter Five the author looks hard at John 4. The Samaritan woman came to draw water alone at noon, when the other women were gone. The author writes, "She was an outcast among outcasts." Then comes the line the chapter turns on: "But Jesus, being weary from His journey, sat by the well, and He waited for her." The author admits she once shut people out, did not answer the door or the phone, and that in her aloneness Jesus came to her well too, through His Word and through prayer.

stories.h2: The radio, the roadside and the fear
paras: In Chapter Four the author remembers being seventeen and driving a big maroon car her friends nicknamed "The Tank." A wave of fear hit her while she listened to pop music, so she switched off the radio, pulled over and prayed to be forgiven. Looking back she writes, "As a true believer, I should never have been so afraid." The chapter uses that memory to ask, with Genesis in view, who told us we were naked, and what fear was handed to us long before we made our own mistakes. In Chapter Seven her father's question comes back: "Are you a victim or a victor?"

paras: The author's dedication explains it. "First, I promised my dad that I would carry the torch of his ministry." "Second, I promised him I would finish my book." She found a Father's Day letter to him folded in his Bible, written after their first reconciliation, which thanked him for pointing her to God.

Of the mistakes she mentions there, she writes, "It was through my divorces and, as a result, the ups and downs of our father-daughter relationship, that we both came to a fuller understanding of the grace of God." faq.q: What is Lessons from the Well about?
faq.a: It is a devotional for the divorced and relationship impaired by Carol Renee Gitthens, a pastor's daughter and mother of five who has been through three marriages and divorces. It combines her story, Scripture and prayer.

faq.q: Does the book include Bible verses for healing?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter lists its Scripture at the start, and chapters quote passages such as "He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3). The Scripture is from the New King James and New American Standard Bibles.

faq.q: What is the woman at the well chapter about?
faq.a: Chapter Five, "Lessons from the Well," is the longest in the book. It looks at John 4, where Jesus waits for a woman the town had pushed to the edges, and it shows what He offered her: Living Water, and a love with no boundaries.

faq.q: Does it justify divorce?
faq.a: No. The foreword says it is not a book that praises or justifies one of the most divisive topics in the church. It points to the healing power of Jesus, despite our choices.

faq.q: Is it a devotional I can use as a journal?
faq.a: Yes. Every chapter closes with Reflections: questions to discuss or journal, lined space to write, Scripture and a prayer.

faq.q: Does it speak to the fear of being abandoned or to feeling worthless after a breakup?
faq.a: The author writes honestly about both. She describes believing she was unworthy after her first heartbreak, and she shows how the woman at the well, and later her own Bible and prayer, answered that belief.

faq.q: Does it speak to being judged by other Christians?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter Eight, "To Judge, or not to Judge, that is the Question," is subtitled "A Plea to Christ Followers." In it she asks, "Why did I feel like I had to make excuses for myself?"

faq.q: Can I use it in a small group or a women's Bible study?
faq.a: Yes. It suits personal study or small group discussion, with questions at the end of each chapter. It is written for women and men who are healing from broken relationships.

stories.h2: A dish that does not look like the picture
paras: The chapter for self-described kitchen failures begins by asking whether your dish failed if it does not look like the one in a cooking magazine. "No way!" is the author's answer. She tells readers that "Perfection is elusive and appearances are just that—appearances," and she makes her point with a tomato: "Not every tomato is worthy of a picture on the cover of a magazine, but every tomato adds flavor to tomato sauce." The lesson is to give yourself grace, learn a few terms and techniques, and grow as you go.

stories.h2: Chicken and dumplings, and cooking for one
paras: Chicken and Dumplings is the first recipe in the book, a simple stew for cold fall days that the author likes to make from scratch. When she taught a friend, Cathy Vau, the hardest part was recognizing when the noodle dough was the right texture. Once you have felt it, the author says, "you'll never forget how to make this dough perfectly." A time-saving tip shows how to use the cooked chicken three ways in one week, and a cooking-for-one tip says that if you make a full pot, "your coworkers will love you."

author.bio: Toni R. Young-Huber grew up on a farm watching her grandmother cook three big meals a day. She lived for a time in the foothills above Denver, where weekend and weeknight guests were common and she learned to stretch a meal. faq.q: What is Get Out of the Fast (Food) Lane! about?
faq.a: It is a warm, practical cookbook of simple, inexpensive recipes with only a few steps, written to help busy people and beginners cook at home instead of using the drive-through.

faq.q: Does it have family dinner ideas?

book.about: There is a profound difference between knowing about God and truly knowing Him. Philip Guenaga grew up in a deeply religious household and moved through several denominations, noticing that the Bible stories stayed the same from church to church while the teaching on salvation changed dramatically: some churches emphasized baptism while others dismissed it, some required speaking in tongues while others called it unnecessary. In Church for 40 Years and Not Knowing God invites readers to set aside inherited assumptions and examine Scripture with fresh eyes. Chapter by chapter he returns to familiar passages: did God name both the first man and the first woman Adam (Genesis 5:2)? What does it mean that male and female were created in God's image? Did Adam and Eve have children in the Garden of Eden? He lays out six pieces of textual evidence, and later chapters ask whether Job's children really died, whether the seals of Revelation have already been opened, and what it means to be born again. The author shares his personal testimony, and a bonus chapter offers a theory on dinosaurs and creation. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes.

paras: Chapter 1 begins with an assumption most readers share, that the first man and woman were named Adam and Eve. The author points to Genesis 5:2: "Male and female created he them; and blessed them, and called their name Adam, on the day when they were created." In his reading, God named them both Adam, the name Eve was given later by the man, and the change reflects a human perspective that developed over time. The chapter closes with reflection questions about how our understanding of gender roles might change if both were first given the same name.

Chapter 5 takes up one of the hardest passages in Scripture. The author looks at the Hebrew word used by each messenger who brings Job bad news, notes that translators rendered it as "servants" in three reports and as "young men" in the fourth, and asks why. He also notices that Job's wife seems distraught only once Job himself is afflicted. He offers a possibility, and he is clear about his purpose: "This perspective doesn't diminish the trials Job endured." The chapter closes with questions about how translation shapes the way we read.

In Chapter 8 the author tells how God changed his life. He grew up in a home where love was absent, one of seven children, and at seventeen he gave his life to God. He writes that "He spoke to me, saying He would be my friend," and that from that moment his life changed. He went on to marry, to serve ten years in the Army and to walk with God through the years. He admits that "some wounds from my childhood linger" and that God continues to heal him. The chapter ends with three questions for the reader about transformation, God's voice and personal struggles that might become testimonies.

He came to Rolla in 1986 and attended the church pastored by Larry Thornhill, who wrote the foreword and says he has known him for 34 years. faq.q: What does the book say about the plan of salvation?
faq.a: Salvation is the issue that opens the book, and Chapter 7, "The Plan of Salvation," asks what it means to be born again. The author says the chapter is not written to condemn any religion or denomination, and that Jesus told Nicodemus the path into the kingdom is to be born again. He writes that the path is "repentance, baptism in Jesus' name, and receiving the Spirit." It is his reading of Scripture, not a denominational statement.

faq.q: What does it say about the story of Job?
faq.a: Chapter 5 compares the Hebrew words used in Job 1 and asks whether Job's children died at all. The author offers it as a possibility to consider and says Job's suffering "was still immense."

faq.q: Does it cover the return of Jesus and the seals of Revelation?
faq.a: Yes. Chapter 6 compares Jesus' words in Matthew 24 with the first five seals of Revelation 6 and asks whether several seals may already have been opened. It does not set dates.

faq.q: What is the image of God, according to the book?
faq.a: Chapter 2 asks what "His image" means when both man and woman were created in it. The author suggests that the union of marriage reflects God's complete image, and he presents it as insight gained through prayer and reflection.

faq.q: Is it good for a Bible study workbook or small group?
faq.a: Yes. Each chapter closes with reflection questions and lined pages for notes, which suits personal study, small groups and Bible classes.

sections.h2: For anyone who wants to read the Bible with fresh expectation
paras: The author believed for decades, as many do, that the Bible was old words about other people. When a friend showed her how God speaks to her in Scripture, it changed everything. Here she shows what that looks like in real moments, with real verses. If you have ever opened your Bible and wondered what it has to do with Tuesday, her stories will give you something to look for.

sections.h2: For believers who want to pray about real decisions
paras: Where to live, whether to sell a home, whether to move a family, how to take an unexpected job: these are the decisions at the center of the book. The author prays about each and tells what she says God said in return. Whatever you think of her interpretations, you will see a woman who asks, listens and checks what she hears against the Bible, which is the habit the book encourages.

sections.h2: For readers who enjoy a warm, honest and humorous Christian memoir
paras: If you like a memoir that is both sincere and funny, you are in the right place. The twins who are nothing alike, the husband who is an engineer and rarely wrong, the baby girl she prayed for, and the day she was lost at Disney World make the pages move quickly. The thirty-four chapters are short enough to read one at a time.

stories.h2: A vision in the night, and a home by February 28
paras: In a rental home the family disliked, the author prayed for help by February 28, the end of the lease. Months later she cried out to God to reveal Himself. Two days after, around 3:00 a.m., she saw a blinding white light in the upper corner of her bedroom, and she writes that she heard, "The whole ordeal you have been through for the last four months will be over very soon." Chapter Five tells what came next. A friend from church called about her house for sale. On the morning of February 28 the author read John 4:50, "You may go, your son will live," and the next word she saw was "pool," and the family bought that home the same day.

For ten years the author had prayed for a baby girl, and she writes that "I had been praying for a baby girl for ten years." On June 19 she asked God to show her in her Bible the word "her" or "she," and it opened to Psalm 87:5. Her husband, an engineer, thought they would have all boys. She kept the promise in her heart through ultrasounds, mailed Christmas cards announcing a girl, and met her daughter three days after the due date. The chapter also tells, honestly, how hard the first months at home were.

stories.h2: An encounter with God in Walmart
paras: On the twenty-first anniversary of a frightening accident in which her son was spared, the author called her older son and asked, for the first time, what he had seen that day. Later, shopping at Walmart, she writes that God said, "For twenty-one years now you have been asking me how you can pay me back for saving your son's life. Let's get something straight; you can't pay me back, so don't ever ask me again." The message she took from it was that she should share the story, and tell others that Jesus died to save their lives eternally.

stories.h2: Day 1: We serve a man of war
paras: Day 1 begins with the verse "The LORD is a man of war; The LORD is His name" from Exodus 15:3. The author reminds readers that when Moses and the Israelites stood at the Red Sea, "they didn't sing praises to their own strength or strategy," but recognized the true source of their victory. Under His command, she says, "we are offensive, not merely defensive; unstoppable, not easily deterred; and victorious, not defeated." The reflection asks you to take inventory of your readiness, to name what you have not yet surrendered and to write a personal declaration of surrender.

Day 5 names fear as the first weapon of the enemy, "because he knows that a frightened soldier cannot fight effectively." The author reminds readers that they stand in a long line of believers: Stephen faced stoning with a face like an angel, and "Paul and Silas sang hymns in prison at midnight." The action for the day is small and practical. Speak truth when it would be easier to stay silent, take a step of faith when you would rather play it safe, and reach out to someone when rejection seems possible. The prayer renounces fear and embraces the spirit of power, love and a sound mind.

stories.h2: Day 9: He is hidden in Christ
paras: Day 9 turns to Colossians. The author writes that when we come to Christ, our old self dies and our new life is hidden in Him, and that "This sacred concealment offers both protection and a new identity." She says the hidden position does not make us ineffective, but gives access to resources beyond human understanding. The reflection asks you to rest in that security today, especially when criticism or attack comes, and to remember that your worth cannot be touched.

author.bio: Patricia Daniel grew up a child of military parents and saw firsthand the discipline, order and commitment of those who served. She has served in multiple ministries over several decades, but most enjoys the Missions ministry, and has served in India and Brazil. She uses her administrative gift, her English as a Second Language certification and her writing gifts to edify the body of Christ. She is the author of three other books: a poetry collection, In Heaven I Can Fly, a children's book, The Purple Swan, and A Block From Grace, a memorial tribute to her parents that she co-authored. Her ministry blog, Destination Jesus, is where she shares her poetry, short stories and Bible teaching. why.title: Why this book exists
paras: It began with a poem. The author writes, "It was not too long ago that I penned a poem called Marching Orders about being prepared to serve faithfully in the end-times." She never imagined it would become the inspiration for a devotional.

She also wrote it because she believes God is preparing believers now. "God is raising up His End-Times Warriors," she writes, "men and women who will dare to believe, trust, and obey Him at ANY COST." She is clear about the limits of the book: "This 40-day devotional by no means captures the full breadth of all God is doing in us and for us in these end-times, but it can serve as a roadmap to help us be ready for His return." Her closing hope is that readers will "rest in the fullness of His grace."

faq.q: What is The End-Times Warrior?
faq.a: A 40-day devotional by Patricia A. Daniel that helps believers prepare to serve Christ as surrendered, fearless warriors and be ready for His return.

faq.q: How is each day built?
faq.a: New King James Scripture and affirmations, a biblical truth, a reflection, ways to apply it, a prayer and journal pages.

faq.q: What are the four sections?

faq.q: Does it include prayers for strength?
faq.a: Each day ends with a written prayer. Day 5, for example, asks the Lord to "Strengthen me to stand fearlessly against every scheme of the enemy," and Day 11 prays that Christ's life will supply what the reader needs.

faq.q: Does it cover the armor of God?

book.about: At five years old, Naggya has already learned to run. In a makeshift hut outside a village in rural Andhra Pradesh, India, his father drinks day and night, and when the money runs out he comes looking for whatever his wife has hidden. One morning Naggya and his mother flee toward the jungle, and she does not survive. Orphaned, he wanders for days in search of the only relative he has ever met, and repeats his mother's words: Son, you must be strong. When his aunt finally finds him she takes him into her single-room hovel, but she is a childless widow, sick, and cannot see how to raise him. Not far away a young man named Elijah has walked away from the philosophies he once preached at university. One encounter with a homeless six-year-old changed everything, and in his parents' mud house he began Son-Shine, a refuge and school for Dalit children. Untouchable is a work of fiction inspired by real events. It opens a window on India's Dalits, the people at the bottom of the traditional caste hierarchy, in a story of cruelty and discrimination and of compassion that reaches one child at a time.

book.short: A short, warm guide from a writer and editor of more than 40 years for people who believe they are not writers: why your story matters, where the words for a book come from and how to start.
book.about: Many people carry a story God has given them but freeze at the thought of writing a book. Carlene Hill Byron, a professional writer and editor for more than 40 years, begins with the most basic question: why write at all? Her answer is that we write to build bridges. Drawing on the old one-lane bridges of her home state of Maine, she shows how stories carry people closer to God and to one another and invites readers to ask what bridge God has prepared them to build. Grounded in Ephesians 2:8-10, the book reminds readers that God is with them, working in and through them, and is not finished with them yet. It explains that the words for a book come from three places: words already written (blogs, sermons, speeches), words found and saved from reading, and words created fresh. It offers simple ways to collect material, from bins and folders by subtopic to journals, 3x5 cards, sticky tabs and online tools, and shares two secrets for facing the blank page. The author uses the example of Joeth Strickland, who began with a few boxes of supplies in her breezeway.

book.about: A Journey Through Grief is a short, compassionate guide for anyone who has lost someone they love and wonders whether life can ever feel right again. Annie Brown writes from more than fifteen years of grief counseling and ministry and from almost thirty-four years of knowing grief personally. Arranged as lessons, each closing with key takeaways, the book describes what grief can look and feel like, the secondary losses that follow a death, the tangled emotions and the endless why and what-if questions, and the temptation to numb pain, which only prolongs the hurt. It addresses anticipated deaths after a long illness as well as sudden tragedies. Throughout, she says there is no right or wrong way to grieve, no schedule and no timeframe, that tears are therapeutic, and that time is not a healer but a great buffer. Rooted in Scripture, including Psalm 23 and Deuteronomy 31:8, it holds that faith sustains us through tragedy. Her message: grief is a process, life will get better, and there is life after death.

book.about: Every parent hopes to raise children who grow into kind, responsible, faithful adults, yet many of the simple habits that once shaped families are quietly disappearing. In Potter's Child, Stephanie Mathews offers ten habits parents can instill in their children, drawn from Scripture, her own life as a mother and the stories of people who have crossed her path. She prayed for years for a baby; when her twins finally arrived they came early, and the first months brought a NICU stay. Each habit is taught through personal testimony and true stories rather than a checklist, including the power of prayer, making your bed and getting the job done, and pitching in with chores at home. The book carries an original poem by Susan Ann Samuel opening each chapter, illustrations by Kalpana Paranjothy and a foreword by Barbara Hemphill. Gaetke was a painfully shy boy who once froze in front of his class; a Sunday School teacher gave him 2 Timothy 1:7 and that verse anchored his life. He went on to build a business career and share his faith with employees, subcontractors and clients. Across twenty-two short chapters in five parts the book covers foundations of faith, mission adventures, why he sold his Porsche and what church planting taught him about multiplication, everyday ministry (his first day in prison, a gas station, a movie theatre, home groups), and reflections on family, stewardship and mentoring, with lessons from Moses, Mary, David and Paul. book.meta: What's Your Word? by Kevin White: ten one-word chapters on choosing life over disaster in Deuteronomy 30, hearing God and acting on the word He gives.
book.short: Pastor and missions leader Kevin White shows how one word from God can redirect your life, through ten one-word chapters from ONE to WORD that begin at God's call in Deuteronomy 30 to choose life.
book.about: On a 1998 trip to India, after ten years in full-time ministry and eighty- and ninety-hour work weeks, Kevin White worshiped with believers in thatch-roof huts who had no bulletins, budgets or Bibles but an undeniable sense of God's presence. On the flight home he committed to pursue God's presence every day, and one word, PRESENCE, rewrote his philosophy of ministry. More words followed: COURAGE, CATCH, FILL. The book is built from ten words, ONE, DISASTER, PROSPERITY, COLLISION, VISION, VALUE, WHY, NOISE, EVERYONE and WORD, each chapter building on the last like colors on a paint-by-number canvas. It begins in Deuteronomy 30, where God sets before His people a choice between life and death, prosperity and disaster, and pleads with them to choose life. Readers learn to notice and act on single words from God, to ask Him for their own word, to tell the words that lead to disaster from the words that lead to prosperity, and to help others find theirs.
who_for: Believers who want to hear God clearly and act on a single word from Him
